speaker: Doctor
text: I see you're experiencing frequent nosebleeds, bleeding from your gums or other mucous membranes, and tiny red spots on your skin called petechiae. To help me understand the cause, have these symptoms been present since birth, or did they start recently?

speaker: Patient
text: 4-year-old male. The child's parent reports that the child has been experiencing frequent episodes of nosebleeds and has had several instances of bleeding from the gums. Additionally, there have been occurrences of unexplained bruising and petechiae, primarily on the distal extremities.

speaker: Doctor
text: Since these symptoms began recently rather than at birth, we need to determine if there are any family members with bleeding disorders. Does anyone in your family have a history of easy bruising or prolonged bleeding after injury?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Frequent epistaxis. I also have Mucous membrane bleeding, Diffuse petechiae on distal extremities.

speaker: Doctor
text: Since the bleeding symptoms are acquired rather than congenital, this points away from hereditary disorders. To evaluate the severity of the platelet dysfunction, I need to see the blood count. REQUEST TEST: Complete_Blood_Count with Platelet_Function_Assay. REQUEST IMAGES: Dermatology_photo_of_petechiae.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Complete_Blood_Count: WBC 6,500 /μL, Hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, Platelets 280,000 /μL (normal); Platelet_Function_Assay: Platelet surfaces deficient in GIIb/IIIa receptors; Dermatology_photo_of_petechiae: Diffuse petechiae noted on the patient's forearms, legs, and a few on his trunk.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Glanzmann's Thrombasthenia.

The platelet count is normal, but the function assay shows a critical deficiency in GIIb/IIIa receptors, which explains the severe mucous membrane bleeding and petechiae despite normal platelet numbers. This confirms a qualitative platelet disorder rather than a quantitative one. No further questions are needed to make this definitive diagnosis.
